name: Nature trivia (hard)
description: 50 hard questions about animals, plants, weather, ecosystems. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: Which animals are the only ones known to detect circularly polarised light?
items.explain: Mantis shrimp can have up to 16 photoreceptor types and are the only animals known to detect circularly polarised light.

source.title: Mantis shrimp have the world's best eyes—but why?

items.question: Mantis shrimp have up to 16 photoreceptor types, while humans have three. How does their colour discrimination compare with ours?
answers: They tell apart about twice as many colours
They tell apart fewer colours than humans do
They tell apart exactly the same colours
They tell apart colours only in ultraviolet
items.correct: They tell apart fewer colours than humans do
items.explain: Despite having more photoreceptor types, mantis shrimp have been found to distinguish fewer colours than humans.

source.title: Rainbow Shrimp Vision Is the Most Powerful of Any Animal on Earth, But We Don’t Know Why

items.question: In the best-sighted mantis shrimp species, how many rows of modified ommatidia form the eye's mid-band?
items.explain: In species with spectacular vision, the middle of the eye has a mid-band of six rows of modified ommatidia.

source.title: Mantis shrimp have the world's best eyes—but why?

items.question: Mantis shrimp are neither mantises nor shrimp. Which animals are their close relatives?
items.explain: Mantis shrimp are marine crustaceans that are close relatives of crabs and lobsters.

source.title: Nature’s Most Amazing Eyes Just Got A Bit Weirder

items.question: Darwin reportedly regarded the Namib Desert plant Welwitschia mirabilis as the botanical counterpart of which animal?
items.explain: Because of its peculiar features, Darwin regarded Welwitschia as the plant equivalent of the platypus.

source.title: Orto Botanico di Napoli - Welwitschia mirabilis

items.question: Which cold, north-flowing ocean current meets hot desert air to create the dense fog that Welwitschia relies on?
items.explain: The regular dense fog forms where the cold Benguela Current meets hot air coming off the Namib Desert.

source.title: Welwitschia mirabilis

items.question: The Afrikaans name for Welwitschia, "tweeblaarkanniedood", literally means what?
answers: Old man of the morning fog
items.explain: The name refers to the plant's two lifelong leaves, which keep growing and are never shed.

source.title: Orto Botanico di Napoli - Welwitschia mirabilis

items.question: Cambridge University Botanic Garden describes Welwitschia mirabilis as a relic of which geological period?
items.explain: The garden says the plant is believed to be a Jurassic relic and the sole surviving member of its family.

source.title: Welwitschia mirabilis - Cambridge University Botanic Garden

items.question: The name of Pando, the giant aspen clone in Utah, is Latin for what?
items.explain: Pando is Latin for "I spread", a nod to the clone's huge root-connected colony.

source.title: Pando - A Forest of One

items.question: How does the quaking aspen mainly propagate itself, producing huge clonal colonies?
items.explain: Quaking aspen spreads primarily through root sprouts, so whole groves can be one genetic individual.

source.title: Populus tremuloides

items.question: In 2006 a clonal colony about 8 km across, perhaps 100,000 years old, was found south of Ibiza. What kind of organism is it?
items.explain: The colony is the seagrass Posidonia oceanica, which may be one of the largest and oldest clonal colonies on Earth.

source.title: Largest organisms

items.question: Which rare Tasmanian shrub survives in the wild as a clonal colony estimated at about 43,600 years old?
items.explain: The wild King's Lomatia colony in Tasmania is a clone estimated to be at least 43,600 years old.

source.title: Clonal colony

items.question: Octopus blood is blue because its oxygen-carrying protein, haemocyanin, contains which metal?
items.explain: Haemocyanin uses copper rather than the iron in our haemoglobin, and it works well in cold, low-oxygen water.

source.title: Octopuses keep surprising us - here are eight examples how

items.question: What are the roles of an octopus's three hearts?
answers: Two supply the arms; one pumps blood past the gills
Two supply the brain; one circulates blood to the arms
Two pump blood past the gills; one supplies the body
Two pump blood to the siphon; one circulates it to the gills
items.correct: Two pump blood past the gills; one supplies the body
items.explain: Two branchial hearts push blood through the gills to pick up oxygen, and the third heart circulates it around the body.

source.title: Octopuses keep surprising us - here are eight examples how

items.question: Roughly what share of an octopus's neurons sit in its eight arms rather than in its brain?
items.explain: About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are spread through its arms, which can taste, smell and grasp on their own.

source.title: Three Hearts, Blue Blood, and Nine Brains: The Octopus Explained (video)

items.question: What happens to octopus blood when it becomes deoxygenated, for example when the animal dies?
answers: It loses its blue colour and turns clear
It turns bright red like ours
It turns green as the copper oxidises
items.correct: It loses its blue colour and turns clear
items.explain: Deoxygenated octopus haemolymph loses its blue colour and becomes clear.

source.title: Octopuses keep surprising us - here are eight examples how

items.question: Francis Beaufort's 1805 wind-force scale was originally devised around which practical matter?
answers: Measuring wave height with a staff
Judging cloud cover from a masthead
items.explain: In 1805 Beaufort described wind force according to the procedures for setting sails on a warship.

source.title: Beaufort Scale - National Geographic Education

items.question: On the Beaufort scale, what is wind of 56–63 knots (Force 11) officially called?
items.explain: The NWS lists Force 11 as winds of 56–63 knots, classed as a violent storm.

source.title: NOAA's National Weather Service - Glossary

items.question: In which year were Forces 13 to 17 added to the Beaufort scale?
items.explain: The original 0–12 scale was extended in 1946 when forces 13 to 17 were added.

source.title: Beaufort scale

items.question: In which year did the US National Weather Service fully implement the Enhanced Fujita scale to replace the original Fujita scale?
items.explain: NOAA's National Weather Service fully implemented the EF scale on February 1, 2007.

source.title: National Weather Service United States Department of Commerce

items.question: What wind-speed estimate range does the Enhanced Fujita scale assign to an EF3 tornado?
items.explain: The NWS lists EF3 (severe tornado) as 136–165 mph.

source.title: National Weather Service United States Department of Commerce

items.question: Ratings on the Enhanced Fujita scale are based solely on the effects of which wind measure on a given damage indicator?
items.explain: Unlike the original Fujita scale, EF ratings are based solely on the effects of 3-second gusts.

source.title: Enhanced Fujita scale

items.question: To fuel its high metabolism, a sea otter must eat roughly what share of its body weight each day?
items.explain: Sea otters have an extremely high metabolism and must consume about 25 percent of their body weight daily.

source.title: The Keystone Species - Catalina Island Marine Institute

items.question: Sea otters keeping urchins in check, which protects kelp and the species that depend on it, is a textbook example of which ecological process?
items.explain: A change in one species, the otter, indirectly affects many others through the food web, which is a trophic cascade.

source.title: Sea Otter: Exploring Keystone Species: HHMI BioInteractive

items.question: In a Monterey Bay study, why did sea otters ignore urchins in urchin barrens but eat those in healthy kelp patches?
answers: Barren urchins were too large to crack open
Barren urchins carried a toxic algal bloom
Barren urchins hid in deep crevices
Barren urchins were starved and nutritionally poor
items.correct: Barren urchins were starved and nutritionally poor
items.explain: Urchins in barrens are starved with little nutritional value, so otters target the well-fed urchins in kelp patches and help sustain them.

source.title: Sea otters maintain remnants of healthy kelp forest amid sea urchin barrens - News

items.question: A 2010 PNAS tracking study found Arctic terns from Greenland and Iceland travelled roughly how far in a year of migration?
items.explain: Tracked terns covered about 70,900 km on average, far above the roughly 40,000 km that had usually been quoted.

source.title: Tracking of Arctic terns Sterna paradisaea reveals longest animal migration

items.question: An Arctic tern ringed as a chick on England's Farne Islands in 1982 reached which city just three months after fledging?
items.explain: The ringed tern reached Melbourne, Australia, in October, a journey of more than 22,000 km.

source.title: Arctic tern

items.question: How many species of periodical cicada (genus Magicicada) are there?
items.explain: There are seven species: four with 13-year cycles and three with 17-year cycles.

source.title: Cicadian Rhythms: Why Does the 17-Year Cicada Emerge Like Clockwork?

items.question: In 2024, a 13-year brood and a 17-year brood of periodical cicadas co-emerged for the first time since which year?
items.explain: Broods XIX and XIII co-emerged in 2024 for the first time since 1803.

source.title: Introduction - Periodical Cicadas: A Resource Guide - Research Guides at Library of Congress

items.question: The survival advantage that periodical cicadas gain by emerging in the billions is known as what?
items.explain: With numbers in the billions, cicadas overwhelm predators, which can only eat a fraction of them.

source.title: Introduction - Periodical Cicadas: A Resource Guide - Research Guides at Library of Congress

items.question: Which fungus genus infects periodical cicadas, staying inactive in the ground until the next emergence years later?
items.explain: The entomopathogenic fungus Massospora cicadina infects both 13- and 17-year cicadas.

source.title: Periodical Cicadas in Ohio

items.question: Periodical cicada nymphs spend nearly all of their 13 or 17 years at roughly what depth, feeding on sap from tree roots?
items.explain: All but a few weeks of the cycle is spent as a nymph 18 to 24 inches deep, feeding on root sap.

source.title: Periodical Cicadas

items.question: In CAM plants, in what form is carbon dioxide stored overnight in the vacuoles before daytime photosynthesis?
items.explain: CO2 taken in through stomata at night is stored as four-carbon malic acid and released again in daylight.

source.title: Crassulacean acid metabolism

items.question: Kranz anatomy is a distinctive leaf structure found in plants using which photosynthetic pathway?
items.explain: Kranz anatomy is unique to C4 plants, just as night-opening stomata are characteristic of CAM plants.

source.title: C4 and CAM photosynthesis

items.question: Symbiotic bacteria inside giant vent tubeworms obtain energy by oxidising which chemical from the vents?
items.explain: The bacteria use hydrogen sulfide from the vents as an energy source in chemosynthesis, feeding themselves and the worm.

source.title: How Giant Tube Worms Survive at Hydrothermal Vents

items.question: The crew of which research submersible found the thriving vent communities that included giant tubeworms?
items.explain: The Alvin crew found the vents and the unexpected tubeworm-filled ecosystem, where life was powered by chemosynthesis.

source.title: How Giant Tube Worms Survive at Hydrothermal Vents

items.question: What is the name of the organ in which a vent tubeworm houses its symbiotic bacteria?
items.explain: The bacteria live in the tubeworm's trophosome, where they oxidise vent chemicals to generate energy.

source.title: Tube Worms

items.question: Giant tubeworms build their protective tube from which material, also found in insect exoskeletons?
items.explain: Tubeworms secrete chitin, which hardens into a protective tube and is extended as the worm grows.

source.title: Tube Worms

items.question: The Dungeness Valley around Sequim, Washington, is unusually dry because it lies in the rain shadow of which range?
items.explain: Sequim and the Dungeness Valley sit in the rain shadow of the Olympic Mountains.

source.title: Rain Shadow deserts

items.question: Death Valley is so hot and dry partly because it sits in the rain shadow of which mountain range?
items.explain: The Sierra Nevada blocks much of the moisture-bearing weather before it reaches Death Valley.

source.title: Rain Shadow

items.question: Of the four major toxins in platypus venom, three belong to which class of proteins?
items.explain: The venom is a cocktail of over 250 chemicals, and three of its four major toxins are defensin-like proteins unique to the platypus.

source.title: Platypus_venom

items.question: Which relative of the platypus has a spur linked to a crural gland that cannot be erected?
items.explain: The echidna's spur is attached to a gland but cannot be erected and used for spurring, unlike the platypus's.

source.title: Echidna Venom Gland Transcriptome Provides Insights into the Evolution of Monotreme Venom

items.question: How does platypus venom differ from snake venom in its effect on tissue?
answers: It seems to lack a tissue-destroying component
items.correct: It seems to lack a tissue-destroying component
items.explain: Unlike snake venom, platypus venom appears to have no necrotising component.

source.title: Platypus venom

items.question: Greenland shark vertebrae lack growth bands, so scientists estimate the shark's age by radiocarbon dating which tissue?
items.explain: The lens of the eye keeps adding layers through life, and radiocarbon dating its centre gives an age estimate.

source.title: Greenland shark, facts and photos

items.question: Greenland sharks reach sexual maturity at roughly what age?
items.explain: A 2016 Science study estimated that Greenland sharks live at least 272 years and reach sexual maturity at about 150.

source.title: Greenland Sharks Are the Longest-Living Vertebrates

items.question: The bombardier beetle Stenaptinus insignis ejects its defensive spray in pulses at about what rate?
items.explain: A study in Science found the spray is ejected in quick pulses at about 500 per second, like a pulse jet.

source.title: Defensive Spray of the Bombardier Beetle: a Biological Pulse Jet

items.question: What is the main component of the bombardier beetle's hot defensive spray?
items.explain: The spray's main component is 1,4-benzoquinone, an irritant to the eyes and respiratory system of vertebrates.

source.title: Bombardier beetle

items.question: Roughly how many times can a bombardier beetle fire its spray before its stored chemicals run out?
items.explain: The beetle's glands store enough hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide for roughly 20 sprays.

source.title: Bombardier beetle

items.question: Which fluid-dynamic phenomenon does the bombardier beetle use to control the direction of its spray?
items.explain: The beetle steers its spray using the Coanda effect, where a fluid flows along the curvature of a surface.

source.title: Fluid ejections in nature
